```{r packages, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(sdmTMB)
```

Penalized complexity (PC) priors (Simpson et al. 2017) shrink a model component towards a simpler base model, with a user-chosen rate of shrinkage.
For a Matérn random field (Fuglstad et al. 2019), the PC prior shrinks towards a base model.
For the range this is a field with an infinite range; for the marginal standard deviation it is a field with no variance.
The joint prior on the range and standard deviation is implemented in `pc_matern()`.
You set each prior with an intuitive statement about the parameter: `pc_matern(range_gt, sigma_lt)` says the range is probably *greater than* `range_gt` and the marginal standard deviation is probably *less than* `sigma_lt`.
With the default `range_prob = 0.05` and `sigma_prob = 0.05`, each statement holds with 95% prior probability.

This article shows PC priors on an isotropic model and on an anisotropic model, where `pc_anisotropy()` (Llamazares-Elias et al. 2024) also shrinks the field towards isotropy.
The anisotropic prior requires the RTMB backend (the default).

## Data and mesh

We use the Pacific cod trawl survey data included with the package.

```{r data}
mesh <- make_mesh(pcod, c("X", "Y"), cutoff = 6)
```

The mesh is reasonably fine relative to the estimated range (about 20 km).
This matters for anisotropy: when the triangles are coarse relative to the range, a fitted model can show strong anisotropy that is an artifact of the mesh.
Check that the estimated anisotropy is stable as the mesh is refined.

## Isotropic model with a PC prior

Coordinates (`X` and `Y`) are in UTM kilometres, so the range is in kilometres.
Here we say the range is probably greater than 10 km and the marginal standard deviation of the field is probably less than 5.
We can see the prior with `plot_pc_matern()`.

```{r plot-pc}
plot_pc_matern(range_gt = 10, sigma_lt = 5)
```

Then fit the model with and without the prior.

```{r fit-iso, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
fit_iso0 <- sdmTMB(
  density ~ 1,
  data = pcod,
  mesh = mesh,
  family = tweedie(),
  spatial = "on"
)

fit_iso <- update(
  fit_iso0,
  priors = sdmTMBpriors(
    matern_s = pc_matern(range_gt = 10, sigma_lt = 5)
  )
)
```

```{r tidy-iso}
tidy(fit_iso0, "ran_pars")
tidy(fit_iso, "ran_pars")
```

The prior is weakly informative: it pulls the range and standard deviation away from implausibly small ranges and large variances, but the data still dominate when they are informative.
The same `matern_st = pc_matern(...)` argument sets a prior on the spatiotemporal field.

## Anisotropic model with PC priors

With `anisotropy = TRUE`, the range can differ by direction.
`pc_anisotropy(ratio_lt)` is a joint prior on the range and the anisotropy that shrinks towards isotropy.
Here we say the ratio of the major to minor axis ranges is probably less than 3.
The range part of the prior still comes from `pc_matern()`, so we supply both.
With anisotropy, `range_gt` refers to the geometric mean of the ranges along the major and minor axes, $\sqrt{\textrm{range}_\textrm{min} \times \textrm{range}_\textrm{max}}$, which is the range $\sqrt{8} / \kappa$ an isotropic field with the same $\kappa$ would have.
The prior on the range depends on the anisotropy: it pushes the range away from small values more strongly when the field is more elongated.
The 5% probability that the geometric mean range is less than 10 km is an average over the prior on the anisotropy ratio; it is higher for nearly isotropic fields (about 9% here) and lower for strongly anisotropic ones (about 1% at a ratio of 3).
The minor-axis range can therefore be below `range_gt`, so choose `range_gt` with the geometric mean in mind rather than the shortest range.

```{r fit-aniso, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
fit_aniso0 <- update(fit_iso0, anisotropy = TRUE)

fit_aniso <- update(
  fit_iso0,
  anisotropy = TRUE,
  priors = sdmTMBpriors(
    matern_s = pc_matern(range_gt = 10, sigma_lt = 5),
    aniso = pc_anisotropy(ratio_lt = 3)
  )
)
```

```{r tidy-aniso}
tidy(fit_aniso0, "ran_pars", conf.int = TRUE)
tidy(fit_aniso, "ran_pars", conf.int = TRUE)
```

The estimated anisotropy can be plotted with `plot_anisotropy()`.
The ellipses show the range in each direction.

```{r plot-aniso}
plot_anisotropy(fit_aniso0)
plot_anisotropy(fit_aniso)
```

Here the data support modest anisotropy, and the prior shrinks it somewhat towards isotropy.
When the data say little about the anisotropy, the unpenalized fit can produce extreme, elongated ellipses, and the prior pulls these towards a circle.
The intervals on `range_min` and `range_max` are unreliable when the ratio is close to 1 (see `?tidy.sdmTMB`).

## Comparing the fits

With anisotropy, the tidy output reports `range_min` and `range_max`: the ranges along the minor and major axes.
Their ratio is the quantity constrained by `pc_anisotropy()`, and their geometric mean is the range that `pc_matern()` refers to.

```{r compare}
get_ranges <- function(fit) {
  x <- tidy(fit, "ran_pars")
  x <- x[x$term %in% c("range_min", "range_max"), ]
  setNames(x$estimate, x$term)
}
r0 <- get_ranges(fit_aniso0)
r1 <- get_ranges(fit_aniso)
round(c(without_prior = unname(r0[2] / r0[1]), with_prior = unname(r1[2] / r1[1])), 2)
```

Log likelihoods and AIC from fits with priors include the penalty and are not comparable with unpenalized fits.

## References

Fuglstad, G.-A., Simpson, D., Lindgren, F., and Rue, H. 2019. Constructing priors that penalize the complexity of Gaussian random fields. Journal of the American Statistical Association 114(525): 445--452. <https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2017.1415907>

Llamazares-Elias, L., Latz, J., and Lindgren, F. 2024. A parameterization of anisotropic Gaussian fields with penalized complexity priors. arXiv:2409.02331. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02331>

Simpson, D., Rue, H., Riebler, A., Martins, T.G., and Sørbye, S.H. 2017. Penalising model component complexity: a principled, practical approach to constructing priors. Statistical Science 32(1): 1--28. <https://doi.org/10.1214/16-STS576>
